1	---
2	name: project-knowledge-harness
3	description: Set up a structured project memory for any software project — TODO.md as priority/effort-tagged index of future work, backlog/ for resume-friendly research/design notes on P? items, and pitfalls/ as a symptom-grep-able knowledge base of past traps. Use when a user wants somewhere to record "maybe later" ideas, freeze troubleshooting state, capture trade-off analysis, or stop re-debugging the same problem.
4	---
5	
6	# project-knowledge-harness
7	
8	A lightweight, file-based memory harness for any software project.
9	
10	Three surfaces, sharply separated by **time direction** and **access pattern**:
11	
12	| Surface | Time | Question it answers | Access pattern |
13	|---|---|---|---|
14	| `TODO.md` | Future | "What might we do later?" | Read top to bottom (priority lanes) |
15	| `backlog/<slug>.md` | Future | "What was the analysis behind this idea?" | Indexed from `TODO.md` |
16	| `pitfalls/<slug>.md` | **Past** | **"I see error X — has this happened before?"** | **Grep symptom keywords** |
17	
18	Plus, in projects that already have agent contracts, `AGENTS.md` Hard
19	invariants answer "What rules MUST agents follow?". Pitfalls *graduate* to
20	Hard invariants when serious enough — see
21	[`references/when-to-add-docs.md`](references/when-to-add-docs.md).
22	
23	## When to use this skill
24	
25	Use this skill when the user surfaces any of:
26	
27	- A long-term TODO list with no home, or a messy `TODO.md` that needs
28	  structure (signals: "where should ideas go?", "maybe later", "工程量太大需要再評估")
29	- A debugging session worth saving (signals: "keep solving the same problem
30	  twice", "save this troubleshooting", "踩過的坑", "TROUBLESHOOTING.md
31	  scattered across docs/")
32	- A request to consolidate `IDEAS.md` / `ROADMAP.md` / `WISHLIST.md` /
33	  `LESSONS.md` files
34	
35	Do NOT use this skill for active sprint planning (use issue trackers),
36	ephemeral agent scratchpads (use `.claude/plans/`), or current feature
37	documentation (use `docs/`).
38	
39	## How to apply this skill (default workflow)
40	
41	The skill bundles five scripts and several templates. **Default to the
42	init script** for setup, and **default to `add-todo.sh` / `sweep-inbox.sh`
43	for capture** rather than asking the agent to edit `TODO.md` by hand.
44	
45	```
46	scripts/
47	  init.sh         # one-shot setup of TODO.md + backlog/ + pitfalls/
48	                  # + agent guidance + README snippet
49	  todo-kanban.sh  # validate TODO.md format and render kanban-style board
50	  add-todo.sh     # insert a structured entry into the right ## P* lane
51	  promote-todo.sh # move an active TODO item to ## Done with the right syntax
52	  sweep-inbox.sh  # triage backlog/inbox.md into TODO.md via add-todo.sh
53	```
54	
55	### 1. Run `scripts/init.sh` against the target repo
56	
57	```sh
58	scripts/init.sh \
59	  --target /path/to/project \
60	  --project-name "My Project" \
61	  --deployment chezmoi   # or npm | pip | docker | none
62	```
63	
64	The script:
65	
66	1. Creates `TODO.md`, `backlog/README.md`, `pitfalls/README.md` from
67	   `assets/*.template`, substituting placeholders.
68	2. Appends an agent-guidance snippet to `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` (auto-detected,
69	   override with `--agent-contract`).
70	3. Appends a "Roadmap & lessons learned" section to `README.md`.
71	4. Runs `scripts/todo-kanban.sh --validate-only TODO.md` so any drift is
72	   caught immediately.
73	5. Prints the deployment-exclusion lines you should add manually (it does
74	   not edit ignore files — see
75	   [`references/deployment-exclusion.md`](references/deployment-exclusion.md)).
76	
77	`init.sh` is idempotent: existing files are skipped unless `--force` is
78	given, and snippets append only if a sentinel marker is missing.
79	
80	### 2. Mid-conversation, when the user surfaces a "maybe later" idea
81	
82	Signals: "maybe later", "nice to have", "if I'm interested",
83	"工程量太大需要再評估", "先記下來", "not now but…".
84	
85	1. If `TODO.md` doesn't exist yet, run `scripts/init.sh` first.
86	2. **Default path — call `scripts/add-todo.sh`** with the priority,
87	   effort, title, and description. This inserts the canonical line into
88	   the right `## P*` lane and re-validates. Add `--backlog` if the
89	   conversation produced enough investigation that a `backlog/<slug>.md`
90	   doc is worth scaffolding.
91	
92	   ```sh
93	   scripts/add-todo.sh --priority "P?" --effort M \
94	     --title "Try Rspress for docs" \
95	     --description "Evaluate AI-native docs framework alternative"
96	   ```
97	
98	3. **Quick-capture path — append to `backlog/inbox.md`** when the user
99	   isn't sure of priority/effort yet, or is mid-thought:
100	
101	   ```sh
102	   echo "- $UNSTRUCTURED_THOUGHT" >> backlog/inbox.md
103	   ```
104	
105	   Later (this session or next), run `scripts/sweep-inbox.sh` to
106	   formalize the loose lines into `TODO.md` one at a time. The sweeper
107	   prompts for missing fields per line; in `--batch` mode it only
108	   processes lines that already have `priority=… effort=… title="…"
109	   description="…"` pairs and leaves ambiguous ones in place.
110	
111	4. **Manual edit path — only when scripts can't help.** Use the syntax
112	   from [`references/tag-schema.md`](references/tag-schema.md) and run
113	   `scripts/todo-kanban.sh --validate-only` afterwards.
114	
115	5. If you wrote a `backlog/<slug>.md` (either via `--backlog` or by
116	   hand), make sure the TODO line ends with
117	   ` → [research](backlog/<slug>.md)` so the index points to the doc.
118	
119	### 3. Mid-conversation, when you finish debugging something tricky
120	
121	Signals: "phew, that took a while", "weird, the error didn't say anything
122	about X", "this is the third time we've hit this", or you find yourself
123	reconstructing context that isn't in any doc.
124	
125	1. Create `pitfalls/<symptom-slug>.md` immediately from
126	   `assets/pitfall-doc.md.template`, while the trace is fresh. Title the
127	   doc by the **symptom**, not the root cause — you'll search by what
128	   you're seeing, not by what you eventually learned.
129	2. Copy verbatim error messages — never paraphrase, it kills grep-ability.
130	3. If the trap is severe (silent corruption / cross-machine recurrence /
131	   non-obvious workaround), surface it: "should this graduate to a Hard
132	   invariant in AGENTS.md?" — see
133	   [`references/when-to-add-docs.md`](references/when-to-add-docs.md).
134	
135	### 4. When implementing a `TODO.md` item
136	
137	In the same commit:
138	
139	1. Run `scripts/promote-todo.sh --title "<substring>" --summary "<what shipped>"`.
140	   It removes the active line and inserts the dated `Done` entry, then
141	   re-validates. It refuses to run if the substring matches zero or more
142	   than one active item.
143	2. If a `backlog/<slug>.md` exists, set its `Status: shipped` (don't
144	   delete — historical record may inform adjacent decisions).
145	3. If shipping uncovered a trap, write a `pitfalls/<slug>.md` for it.
146	
147	## When a TODO entry needs a `backlog/` doc, when a debug needs a `pitfalls/` doc
148	
149	Decision rules and the upgrade path to `AGENTS.md` invariants live in
150	[`references/when-to-add-docs.md`](references/when-to-add-docs.md). Read it
151	the first time you set up the harness; consult it again whenever you're
152	unsure which surface a piece of knowledge belongs in.
153	
154	## Tag schema
155	
156	Two orthogonal axes, validated by `scripts/todo-kanban.sh`. See
157	[`references/tag-schema.md`](references/tag-schema.md) for the full schema,
158	useful tag combinations, and the exact validator-checked syntax.
159	
160	## Anti-patterns
161	
162	Common mistakes to avoid (e.g., spawning `IDEAS.md` alongside `TODO.md`,
163	titling pitfalls by root cause, paraphrasing errors). Full list in
164	[`references/anti-patterns.md`](references/anti-patterns.md).
165	
166	## Deployment exclusion
167	
168	`TODO.md`, `backlog/`, and `pitfalls/` are maintainer-facing repo metadata,
169	not files to ship. Cheatsheet for chezmoi / npm / pip / Docker in
170	[`references/deployment-exclusion.md`](references/deployment-exclusion.md).
171	`scripts/init.sh --deployment ...` prints the exact lines to add.
172	
173	## Templates and bundled assets
174	
175	- `assets/TODO.md.template` — `TODO.md` skeleton with example items per lane
176	- `assets/backlog-README.md.template` — `backlog/` index + when-to-add rules
177	- `assets/backlog-doc.md.template` — single backlog doc (context-first)
178	- `assets/pitfalls-README.md.template` — `pitfalls/` index + cross-reference
179	  table for traps documented elsewhere
180	- `assets/pitfall-doc.md.template` — single pitfall doc (symptom-first)
181	- `assets/agent-guidance.md.template` — snippet for `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`
182	- `assets/readme-roadmap.md.template` — snippet for project `README.md`
183	- `scripts/init.sh` — one-shot setup
184	- `scripts/todo-kanban.sh` — validator + Markdown kanban renderer
185	  (also supports `--json` and `--validate-only`)
186	- `scripts/add-todo.sh` — structured insert into `## P*` lane;
187	  `--backlog` also scaffolds `backlog/<slug>.md`
188	- `scripts/promote-todo.sh` — atomic active-→-Done move with re-validation
189	- `scripts/sweep-inbox.sh` — triage `backlog/inbox.md` → `add-todo.sh`
190	
191	## Reference implementation
192	
193	A live example of this harness is at
194	[`daviddwlee84/dotfiles`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles):
195	
196	- `TODO.md`, `backlog/`, `pitfalls/` directories at repo root
197	- `AGENTS.md` `### Long-term backlog → TODO.md + backlog/` and
198	  `### Past pitfalls → pitfalls/` sections
199	- `README.md` `## Roadmap & lessons learned` section

```text
# Pueue Common Pitfalls and Debugging Guide

Based on the documentation, here are the key troubleshooting approaches:

## Diagnostic Steps

**Initial Testing**: Before assuming Pueue is the problem, run your command directly using `sh -c '$COMMAND'` to isolate whether the issue stems from the command itself or Pueue's task management.

**Output Inspection**: Use `pueue log $task_id` for reviewing task output, or `pueue follow $task_id` to monitor execution in real-time.

## Common Problem Areas

**Shell Syntax Issues**: Characters requiring escaping need proper quoting. For example, paths with spaces demand encapsulation as strings to preserve escape sequences when passed to background processes.

**Interactive Prompts**: Processes expecting user responses can receive input through the `pueue send` command. Alternatively, many tools offer non-interactive flags (like `--yes`) that bypass confirmation requests.

**Shell Aliases**: Custom aliases from rc files aren't supported; Pueue provides its own aliasing system as an alternative.

**GUI Programs**: Applications requiring display servers or window managers will fail in Pueue's background execution environment.

## Platform-Specific Considerations

On Windows, daemonization (`pueued --daemonize`) may not behave reliably—the daemon could terminate when closing the terminal, or Ctrl+C in certain contexts might inadvertently shut down the daemon. These issues were addressed in version 4.0+.
```

```text
# Pueue Configuration Overview

## Configuration File Locations

Pueue stores its default configuration in platform-specific directories:

- **Linux**: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pueue/pueue.yml` or `~/.config/pueue/pueue.yml`
- **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/pueue.yml`
- **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\pueue\pueue.yml`

The daemon automatically generates a default configuration file on first launch. You can override the location using the `-c` command-line flag or the `PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable (the flag takes precedence).

## Key Configuration Sections

**Shared Settings** control socket/network behavior:
- `use_unix_socket`: Enable Unix sockets (Unix systems only)
- `unix_socket_path`: Socket location
- `host` and `port`: TCP connection details
- `pueue_directory`: Storage location for logs and intermediate files

**Client Settings** affect the command-line interface:
- `dark_mode`: Color scheme option
- `read_local_logs`: Local disk access instead of socket transmission
- `status_time_format`: Custom time display formatting

**Daemon Settings** govern task execution:
- `pause_group_on_failure`: Halt queued tasks in the failed task's group
- `callback`: Execute commands after task completion
- `shell_command`: Specify custom shell execution environment
- `env_vars`: Inject environment variables into all tasks

## Profiles

Multiple configuration profiles can coexist in one file, selectable via command line: `pueue --profile remote status`. This enables managing different daemon instances or remote connections from a single configuration file.
```

```text
# Pueue: Task Queue Management Tool

## Overview

Pueue is a command-line task management system that processes a queue of shell commands with both sequential and parallel execution capabilities. The project is written in Rust and is considered feature-complete.

## Key Features

**Task Scheduling:**
- Add tasks progressively and control concurrent execution limits
- Reorder queued tasks and establish dependencies between them
- Schedule tasks for specific execution times

**Process Management:**
- Inspect task output easily
- Send input to running processes
- Pause/resume individual tasks or groups

**Background Execution:**
- The `pueued` daemon runs persistently without requiring active login sessions
- Tasks execute in their original working directories with copied environment variables
- Full shell feature support for command execution

**Data Persistence:**
- Queue state saves to disk and survives system crashes
- Task logs persist permanently

**Cross-Platform Support:**
- Fully functional on Linux, macOS, and Windows

## Installation Methods

- **Package Manager:** Preferred approach with automatic service file and completion deployment
- **Prebuilt Binaries:** Available for Linux (including ARM), macOS, and Windows
- **Cargo:** `cargo install --locked pueue`
- **From Source:** Clone repository and build with `cargo build --release`

## Design Philosophy

Pueue deliberately avoids distributed task management, multi-user support, and extensive scripting features. The tool prioritizes human interaction and simplicity over heavy-duty programmatic control.

## Community

The project maintains active development with 6.2k GitHub stars, 155 forks, and welcomes community contributions through the main branch workflow.
```

# Pueue Wrapper: Dependencies and Entry Points

## Project Overview
This is a Python package called `pueue_wrapper` (v0.2.5) that requires Python 3.12 or later and serves as a wrapper for Pueue, a task queue system.

## Core Dependencies
The project relies on several key libraries:

- **loguru** (≥0.7.3): Logging framework
- **pydantic** (≥2.11.0): Data validation using Python type hints
- **tyro** (≥0.8.14): CLI argument parser
- **uvicorn** (≥0.34.0): ASGI server implementation

## API & UI Components
Since the API and UI are integrated into the package, additional dependencies include:

- **fastapi** (≥0.115.12): Web framework for building APIs
- **streamlit** (≥1.49.0): Framework for data applications
- **plotly** (≥5.0.0): Interactive visualization library
- **watchdog** (≥6.0.0): File system event monitoring

## Command-Line Entry Points
Two executable scripts are provided:

1. `pueue-api-server`: Launches the API server via the module `pueue_wrapper.api.run_api_server:cli`
2. `pueue-ui-server`: Launches the UI server via the module `pueue_wrapper.ui.run_ui_server:cli`

## Development & Build
The project uses **black** (≥25.1.0) for code formatting and **hatchling** as its build backend, with packages located in `src/pueue_wrapper`.
```

# PueueWrapper Repository Structure

This is a Python project providing a wrapper interface for **Pueue**, a command queue management tool. Here's the repository organization:

## Core Directories

**`src/pueue_wrapper/`** - Main package containing:
- **`core/`** - Async and sync implementations for queue operations
- **`models/`** - Pydantic data models for tasks, groups, status, and logs
- **`api/`** - REST API server for programmatic access
- **`ui/`** - Streamlit-based web interface with multiple pages (task submission, management, statistics, group management, logs, templates, and help)
- **`extensions/`** - Advanced features including statistics and utilities

## Supporting Files

- **`pyproject.toml`** & **`uv.lock`** - Dependency and project configuration using `uv` package manager
- **`.python-version`** - Python version specification
- **`.cursor/` & `.vscode/`** - IDE configuration and development rules
- **`.specstory/`** - Project documentation history with detailed technical specifications

## Documentation & Examples

- **`docs/`** - Feature documentation, UI guides, test results
- **`examples/`** - Usage demonstrations for async/sync features and UI testing
- **`README.md`, `TODO.md`** - Project overview and task tracking

The project emphasizes providing both programmatic (Python API, REST API) and graphical (Streamlit UI) interfaces for managing Pueue job queues.

```text
# Pueue: Command-Line Task Queue Manager

**Pueue** is a CLI tool that manages sequential and parallel execution of long-running shell commands through a queue system.

## Core Functionality

Pueue operates as a daemon (`pueued`) that processes queued tasks in the background, allowing you to control execution from any terminal without maintaining an active session. The queue persists to disk and survives system crashes.

## Key Features

**Scheduling capabilities:**
- Add tasks progressively
- Run multiple tasks concurrently (configurable)
- Reorder queued tasks
- Set task dependencies
- Schedule tasks for specific times

**Process management:**
- Inspect task output
- Send input to running processes
- Pause/resume individual tasks or groups
- Kill tasks selectively

**Task organization:**
- Group-based queue management
- Multiple parallel tasks per group
- Pause/start by group

**Data persistence:**
- Queue saved to disk automatically
- Log files persist across crashes
- JSON output for programmatic access

## Installation Methods

- **Package managers** (preferred, auto-deploys service files)
- **Prebuilt binaries** for Linux, macOS, Windows
- **Cargo**: `cargo install --locked pueue`
- **From source** via Git clone and `cargo build`

## Command Structure

The tool uses subcommands like `add`, `status`, `log`, `follow`, `pause`, `restart`, and `wait` to manage tasks.

## Design Philosophy

Pueue deliberately remains "feature-complete" and intentionally excludes distributed task management, multi-user systems, and heavy scripting support—positioning itself as a single-user convenience tool rather than an enterprise scheduler.
```

```text
# Pueue: Task Queue Manager

**Pueue** is a command-line tool for managing sequential and parallel execution of long-running shell commands. It operates as a background daemon that processes queued tasks independently of active terminal sessions.

## Key Capabilities

The tool supports:
- **Task scheduling** with concurrent execution limits and dependency management
- **Process interaction** including output inspection and pause/resume functionality
- **Task groups** (multiple queues) with individual concurrency settings
- **Background execution** via the `pueued` daemon with environment variable preservation
- **Data persistence** with automatic recovery from crashes
- **Cross-platform support** for Linux, macOS, and Windows

## Design Philosophy

Pueue is intentionally kept simple and is considered feature-complete. The project explicitly avoids:
- Distributed task management
- Multi-user task coordination
- Sophisticated load-balancing algorithms
- Extensive scripting APIs (though `pueue-lib` exists for programmatic access)

As stated: "Pueue is designed to be a convenient helper tool for a single user."

## Installation Options

Users can install via:
- Package managers (preferred method)
- Pre-built binaries from GitHub releases
- Cargo (`cargo install --locked pueue`)
- Building from source using stable Rust

The project is written in Rust and includes 2,017+ commits with active maintenance and 6.2k GitHub stars.
```

# SQLite local mode (recommended for solo experiments)

> Authoritative source: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/tracking/backend-stores.html

The "DVC-like but more flexible" sweet spot: one local file (`mlflow.db`), full
UI, model registry support, no Docker. Trade-off: serialized writes — single-user only.

# In your project root:

```

1. Touches `mlflow.db` if missing
2. Adds `mlflow.db`, `mlruns/`, `mlartifacts/` to `.gitignore`
3. Prints the tracking URI and the `mlflow ui` command

# PueueAsyncCore - Main Methods Overview

## Basic Task Operations
- **add_task()** - Queues a command with optional parameters like priority, dependencies, delay, and group assignment
- **wait_for_task()** - Blocks until a specific task completes
- **remove_task()** - Deletes tasks from the queue
- **kill_task()** - Terminates running tasks or all tasks in a group
- **pause_task()** - Suspends task execution at the task or group level
- **start_task()** - Resumes or initiates tasks or group execution
- **restart_task()** - Reruns tasks with optional in-place restart
- **clean_tasks()** - Removes finished tasks from the list
- **reset_queue()** - Clears all tasks, optionally limited to specific groups

## Status & Query Operations
- **get_status()** - Retrieves current queue state and task statuses
- **get_log()** - Fetches task output as plain text
- **get_logs_json()** - Returns structured task logs in JSON format
- **get_task_log_entry()** - Extracts a single task's log data

## Group Management Operations
- **get_groups()** - Lists all groups and their configurations
- **add_group()** - Creates a new task group
- **remove_group()** - Deletes a group with optional task cleanup
- **set_group_parallel()** - Configures concurrent task limits per group
```

# TaskAddOptions and TaskControl Classes

## TaskAddOptions
This class defines configuration options when adding a task:

**Fields:**
- `working_directory`: Optional directory path for task execution
- `escape`: Boolean flag for escaping behavior
- `immediate`: Boolean to execute task immediately
- `follow`: Boolean to follow task progress
- `stashed`: Boolean to mark task as stashed
- `delay`: Optional time delay before execution
- `group`: Optional group identifier
- `after`: Optional list of task IDs that must complete first
- `priority`: Optional integer priority level
- `label`: Optional string label for the task
- `print_task_id`: Boolean to output the task identifier

## TaskControl
This class represents "Task control operation result" and contains:

**Fields:**
- `success`: Boolean indicating operation success
- `message`: Optional status or error message
- `task_ids`: Optional list of affected task identifiers

Both classes use Pydantic's `BaseModel` for validation and data management.

# Task and PueueStatus Data Classes

## Task Class
Captures individual task metadata:
- **Identifiers**: `id`, `created_at`
- **Execution**: `original_command`, `command`, `path`, `envs` (environment variables)
- **Organization**: `group`, `dependencies`, `priority`, `label`
- **State**: `status` dictionary containing task status information

## PueueStatus Class
Represents the complete queue system state:
- **Collections**: `tasks` (task ID to Task mapping) and `groups` (group name to Group mapping)
- **Utility methods**: Helper functions to retrieve tasks by status type (running, done, queued, failed) and generate status counts

The PueueStatus class essentially wraps "the complete response from `pueue status --json`" along with convenience methods for filtering and analyzing tasks across different states.

# Analysis of `wait_for_task` Method

## Method Overview

The `wait_for_task` method is defined as:

```python
def wait_for_task(self, task_id: str) -> str:
    """
    Waits for a specific task to finish synchronously.
    
    Args:
        task_id: ID of the task to wait for
    
    Returns:
        str: Command output
    """
    return self._run_async_method("wait_for_task", task_id)
```

## Key Characteristics

**Synchronous Wrapper**: This method wraps an async operation through the `_run_async_method` helper, which handles event loop management intelligently. It detects whether an event loop is already running and either uses `asyncio.run()` or executes the call in a separate thread via `ThreadPoolExecutor`.

**Blocking Behavior**: The method blocks until the specified task completes, returning the command's output as a string.

## Polling/Timeout Patterns

The provided code snippet does not reveal explicit timeout or polling mechanisms within `wait_for_task` itself. The implementation delegates to the async layer (`PueueAsyncCore`), whose internals aren't shown here. Timeout handling would likely occur at the async method level rather than in this synchronous wrapper.

## Pueue `--after` Flag Dependency Semantics

A dependency can be specified by using the --after/-a flag on the add command.

### How Dependencies Work

Tasks with this option will only be started, if all specified dependencies successfully finish. Tasks with failed dependencies will fail as well.

More specifically, a task will only be executed if all dependencies were successful.

### Task States

When dependencies fail, Pueue uses specific task states to track the situation:
- A new state DependencyFailed is used if any dependency of a task fails.

### Usage Context

It is advised to use this in combination with the pause_on_failure setting. This configuration prevents the daemon from starting new tasks when any task fails, which can help you manage dependent task chains.

The `--after` flag takes task IDs as arguments to specify which tasks must complete successfully before the new task will be executed.

# Task Management Patterns in Pueue

## Task Creation

The code demonstrates task creation using the `PueueWrapper`:

```python
task1 = await pueue.add_task('echo "Hello, World!"', "问候任务")
task2 = await pueue.add_task('sleep 2 && echo "Done sleeping"', "睡眠任务")
task3 = await pueue.add_task("ls -la", "列表任务")
```

Each task accepts a command string and an optional label describing its purpose.

## Waiting for Completion

The implementation uses a simple asynchronous pause:

```python
await asyncio.sleep(3)
```

# Pueue 0.7.1 Overview

Pueue is a command-line task management tool designed for executing long-running shell commands sequentially or in parallel. The project is written in Rust and available on crates.io.

## Core Functionality

The tool enables users to queue shell commands for execution in their respective working directories. Key features include:

- **Task scheduling** with output inspection capabilities
- **Process interaction** including pause/resume functionality
- **Parallel execution** with configurable concurrency limits
- **Task grouping** where each group maintains its own queue with independent parallelism settings
- **Callback hooks** for desktop notifications or post-task actions
- **Cross-platform support** for Linux, macOS, and partial Windows compatibility

## Architecture

Pueue operates as a client-daemon system. The daemon (`pueued`) runs continuously in the background, processing the task queue independently of terminal sessions. Users interact through the client (`pueue`), allowing remote task management from any terminal on the same machine.

## Configuration

The system stores configuration in `pueue.yml` with settings for daemon port, parallelism defaults, and task callbacks. Users can define task groups with different resource allocations—useful for separating I/O-intensive tasks from CPU-bound work.

## Use Cases

The tool addresses scenarios involving bulk data operations, compression tasks, video encoding, and lengthy file transfers where traditional terminal approaches become unwieldy.

Based on the search results, I found information about the `pueue restart` command with the flags you're asking about:

## Pueue Restart Command

The `restart` command restarts failed or successful task(s). By default, identical tasks will be created and enqueued, but it's possible to restart in-place.

### Flags Explained

- **`--in-place`**: Restarts a task in-place without enqueuing as a separate task

- **`--start-immediately`**: This flag causes the restarted task to begin execution immediately rather than being queued

### Usage

The syntax is: `pueue restart --start-immediately [task_id] [task_id]` to restart specific tasks, or `pueue restart --in-place [task_id]` to restart a task in-place

### Note on Recent Changes

In version 4.0.0 and later, the `--immediate` flag is allowed instead of `--start-immediately` on pueue restart for consistency with pueue add.

When combining both flags together as `pueue restart --in-place --start-immediately [task_id]`, you're restarting a task in-place while also making it start immediately without waiting in the queue. After the task is restarted, it receives a new task ID from the system.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# SCRIPT_NAME — one-line description.
# Bash 3.2 compatible (works on stock macOS).

usage() {
  cat <<'EOF'
Usage: SCRIPT_NAME [OPTIONS] ARGS
[paragraph description]

warn() { printf 'warn: %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
die()  { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit "${2:-1}"; }

  # Emit structured data on stdout; diagnostics on stderr.
}

## PueueWrapper Abstractions Report

**High-Level Operations:**
The wrapper exposes: task submission (`add_task`), task waiting (`wait_for_task`), group management (create/remove groups, set parallel concurrency per group), and lifecycle operations (restart, kill, pause, start, clean). All operations have both async (`PueueAsyncCore`) and sync (`PueueSyncCore`) variants.

**Dependency Model:**
PueueWrapper wraps Pueue's native `--after` dependency system directly. `TaskAddOptions.after` accepts a list of task IDs that must complete before the task runs—this enables simple sequential DAGs but not arbitrary dependency scheduling. No custom scheduler is built; the abstraction just exposes Pueue's CLI-native feature.

**Status Data Classes:**
Pydantic models parse `pueue status --json`:
- `Task`: captures id, command, group, dependencies, priority, label, status dict, path, environment variables
- `Group`: group metadata (name, config, parallel limits)
- `PueueStatus`: wraps full queue state as a dict of task_id→Task, group_name→Group, plus convenience methods like `.get_running_tasks()`, `.get_done_tasks()`, etc.
- `TaskAddOptions`: configuration for submission (working_dir, delay, group, after, priority, label, stashed)

**Waiting Patterns:**
`wait_for_task(task_id)` blocks until completion. The sync wrapper handles this by delegating to the async layer, which polls Pueue's CLI. No explicit timeout is exposed in the public API; polling happens via internal async methods. Group-level draining is implicit—you check status after cleanup operations.

**Entry Points:**
Two CLI commands: `pueue-api-server` (FastAPI REST wrapper) and `pueue-ui-server` (Streamlit web UI). Python API is through `PueueWrapper` (async) or `PueueWrapperSync` (blocking). No bespoke task pool or parallel executor abstraction—parallelism is group-level via `set_group_parallel()`.

**Key Pattern:**
Task organization centers on **groups** with configurable concurrency, lightweight **linear dependencies** via `after`, and **simple polling** through status queries. The wrapper is thin—it's a CLI bridge, not a job orchestrator.

# pueue-add Command Overview

**pueue-add** is a Linux utility for managing task queues. According to the documentation, it "adds a new command to the task queue. Commands are queued and executed in order."

## Key Options

The command supports several useful flags:

- **-i / --immediate**: Launch the task right away rather than waiting
- **-g / --group**: Assign the task to a specific group
- **--delay**: Schedule execution after a specified duration (e.g., "10min")
- **--stashed**: Add the task in paused state
- **-l / --label**: Attach a descriptive label to the task
- **-a / --after**: Create dependencies on other task IDs
- **-p / --priority**: Set task priority level

## Basic Usage

The fundamental syntax is: `pueue add [options] command`

For example, you can queue a command with `pueue add [command]`, or add it with priority handling and dependencies using the appropriate flags.

The tool is particularly useful for batch job scheduling and managing multiple processes in an organized queue system.

Based on the search results, here's the information about the Pueue daemon socket location:

## Default Unix Socket Path

The Unix socket path configuration defaults to runtime_directory/pueue_$USER.socket.

## Runtime Directory Location

The runtime directory is used for runtime variables and defaults to pueue_directory or $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.

## Configuration

On Unix systems, you can configure whether the daemon should listen on a Unix socket or TCP socket. The socket location can be customized through the configuration file under the `unix_socket_path` setting.

## Example Socket Paths

From the configuration documentation, example socket paths include:
- `~/.local/share/pueue/pueue_your_user.socket` (as shown in the default config example)
- `/run/user/0/pueue_root.socket` (for root user with $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR)

You can override the socket path via the command line using the `-u` or `--unix-socket-path` option when running the pueue client.

## Task Log Location

All logs can be found in ${pueue_directory}/logs.

## Accessing Task Output

pueue log displays the captured stdout and stderr output of pueue tasks, both running and finished. By default it shows the last few lines; use --full to see complete output or --lines to control the number of lines displayed.

The basic command to view logs is:
- `pueue log` - to display log output of finished tasks
- `pueue log $task_id` - to see the output of a specific task

You can also use the `-f` flag to follow running output and the `-e` flag to follow stderr specifically.

## Log Persistence

Logs of previous Pueue sessions will be created whenever you issue a reset or clean. This means your logs are preserved across daemon restarts and session changes.

Based on the search results, here's the information about pueue's default group behavior when you omit the `--group` flag:

## Default Group Behavior

If no group is specified, the task will just be added to the default queue.

Several pueue commands operate on the "default" group when the `--group` flag is omitted:

- **start/resume**: By default, this resumes the default group and all its tasks.
- **pause**: By default, pauses the default group and all its tasks.
- **kill**: Kills all tasks of the default group when no ids or a specific group are provided.
- **wait**: By default, this will wait for all tasks in the default group to finish.
- **parallel**: By default, adjusts the amount of the default group.

In summary, when you omit the `--group` flag in pueue commands, operations target the "default" group by default, which is a built-in group that exists automatically in all pueue installations.

I found relevant information about Pueue's environment variable passthrough feature. Here are the key findings:

## Environment Variables Passthrough in Pueue

Pueue preserves the current environment variables when calling `pueue add`, ensuring that the command behaves as close as possible to executing it in the shell right then and there.

### PUEUE_WORKER_ID and PUEUE_GROUP Variables

Pueue leaks a representation of its internal worker pool to called commands via the `$PUEUE_WORKER_ID` environment variable, which represents the current "worker" a task is assigned to. There will never be two concurrent tasks with the same `$PUEUE_WORKER_ID` in the same group.

Additionally, `$PUEUE_GROUP` is the name of the group the task is currently in.

### Use Case Example

The task's group name and the pool's worker id for a given task are injected into the environment variables of the subprocess, allowing users to map Pueue's internal group and worker logic to external resources with commands like `./run_on_gpu_pool --gpu $PUEUE_WORKER_ID --pool $PUEUE_GROUP`

This feature enables tasks to be aware of which worker they're assigned to and which group they belong to during execution, which is particularly useful for resource allocation and scheduling purposes.

# Pueue Changelog - Recent Notable Changes

Based on the changelog, here are significant recent developments:

## Version 4.0.0 (2025-03-09) - Major Redesign

**Task State Refactoring**: The internal task state representation was completely overhauled using Rust's struct enums to "enforce various invariants during compile time via the type system." This broke backwards compatibility with pre-v4.0 states.

**Editing Improvements**: Task editing was redesigned to support two approaches - a file-based system and TOML format - allowing "editing all properties a task in one editor session" rather than opening multiple editor windows.

**Process Command Responsiveness**: Commands affecting subprocess states now "only return when the task is actually started/stopped/paused," eliminating previous delays that caused issues with command chaining.

**Windows Service Support**: "Added Windows service on Windows to allow a true daemon experience."

**State Compression**: New option to "save the state in compressed form," showing compression ratios up to 15x on large task queues.

## Version 3.4.0 (2024-03-22)

Added priority modification capabilities via `pueue edit --priority` and support for unlimited parallel tasks by setting `parallel_tasks` to `0`.

## Key Breaking Changes

The v4.0.0 release introduced significant backwards-incompatible modifications to the protocol, data format handling, and CLI interfaces to improve the overall architecture and user experience.

Perfect. Now let me compile my research findings into a comprehensive report.

## Research Report: Pueue Command Surface for Agent Integration

Based on documented sources from pueue's GitHub repository, wiki, and official documentation, here is what an LLM agent needs to know:

### 1. **Core Lifecycle Commands**

- **`pueue add [command]`** enqueues a task. Key flags (from man pages):
  - **`-l / --label TEXT`**: Attach a descriptive label (displayed in `pueue status`)
  - **`-a / --after <TASK_ID>`**: Create dependency (see #3)
  - **`-g / --group <GROUP>`**: Assign to group (defaults to "default" group if omitted)
  - **`-i / --immediate`**: Start task right away instead of queuing
  - **`--stashed`**: Add in paused state (won't auto-start)
  - **`--delay <DURATION>`**: Schedule execution later (e.g., "10min")
  - **`-p / --priority <NUM>`**: Set task priority
  - **`--escape`**: Escape special characters in command strings
  - **`--print-id`**: Output the new task ID to stdout
  - Tasks execute in "their original working directories with copied environment variables" (no explicit `--working-directory` flag documented)

- **`pueue pause [--group G]`**, **`pueue start [--group G]`**: Pause/resume tasks or groups
- **`pueue kill [task_ids]`**, **`pueue remove [task_ids]`**: Terminate or remove tasks
- Environment variables **`$PUEUE_WORKER_ID`** and **`$PUEUE_GROUP`** are injected into task execution (worker pool assignment and group name)

### 2. **Groups and Parallelism**

- **`pueue group add <NAME>`**: Create a new group
- **`pueue group remove <NAME>`**: Delete a group  
- **`pueue parallel <N> [--group G]`**: Set parallel concurrency (can be unlimited if set to `0`)
- When `--group` is omitted, the "default" group is used automatically
- Default group is built-in; no creation needed
- Groups allow resource segregation (e.g., one `io` group at 1 task, `cpu` group at 2 tasks in parallel)

### 3. **Dependencies / DAG Support**

- **`--after <TASK_ID>`** (short: **`-a`**) is the dependency flag on `pueue add`
- **Semantics**: "Tasks with this option will only be started if all specified dependencies successfully finish. Tasks with failed dependencies will fail as well."
- **No success/failure distinction**: Dependencies run only on success; failed parent → dependent marked with **`DependencyFailed`** status
- Use with **`pause_group_on_failure`** config setting to prevent new tasks from starting when any task fails

### 4. **JSON / Scripting Surface**

- **`pueue status --json`** and **`pueue log --json`** (short: **`-j`**) support JSON output
- **Available fields** (from docs.rs and usage): JSON output includes task `id`, `status`, `label`, `group` 
- **Documentation gap**: Exact JSON schema for `dependencies`, `exit_code`, `start_time`, `end_time` fields not explicitly documented in fetched sources; recommend running `pueue status --json | jq` to inspect actual output structure
- **No `--print-task-id` explicitly documented**; `--print-id` is the actual flag for stdout output (format undocumented)

### 5. **Retry / Restart**

- **`pueue restart [--in-place] [--start-immediately] [task_ids]`**
- **`--in-place`**: Restart task in its current queue position without creating a new entry
- **`--start-immediately`** (also **`--immediate`** in v4.0+): Begin execution immediately
- Default behavior (without flags): Creates a new task ID with identical command (does not reuse old ID)
- New task ID is assigned even with `--in-place --start-immediately`

### 6. **Output Retrieval**

- **`pueue log [task_id]`**: Display captured stdout/stderr (shows last few lines; use `--full` for complete output or `--lines N`)
- **`pueue follow [task_id]`**: Monitor running task output in real-time
- **Log storage**: All logs reside in **`${pueue_directory}/logs`** (e.g., `~/.local/share/pueue/logs/` on Linux)
- **No explicit stdout-only vs stderr-only flags documented** (follow flag `-e` for stderr mentioned but not fully specified)

### 7. **Daemon Lifecycle**

- **`pueued`**: Start daemon; use **`-d` or `--daemonize`** for background mode
- **Socket path**: Defaults to **`runtime_directory/pueue_${USER}.socket`** (e.g., `~/.local/share/pueue/pueue_username.socket` or `/run/user/{uid}/pueue_{user}.socket` if `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` set)
- **Config file**: Platform-specific:
  - Linux: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pueue/pueue.yml` or `~/.config/pueue/pueue.yml`
  - macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/pueue.yml`
  - Windows: `%APPDATA%\pueue\pueue.yml`
- **Daemon required**: All `pueue` client commands require a running `pueued` daemon (socket communication)
- **Config can be overridden**: `-c` flag or `PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable

### 8. **Agent Gotchas**

1. **Default group behavior**: Omitting `--group` targets "default" group; no explicit creation needed
2. **Task failure → dependents fail**: If parent task fails, all tasks with `--after parent_id` are marked `DependencyFailed` and do not execute
3. **`pueue add` stdout unclear**: `--print-id` outputs the task ID, but exact format (plain integer vs JSON) is **not documented**; agent should test or use `pueue status --json` for reliable parsing
4. **Command escaping required**: "The command needs proper shell escaping"; recommend wrapping in single quotes or using `--escape` flag
5. **No shell aliases**: Custom rc-file aliases are not available in pueued environment; use pueue's own aliasing system (`pueue_aliases.yml`)
6. **`pause_group_on_failure` is config-level**: Not a command-line flag; must be set in `pueue.yml` to auto-pause group on task failure
7. **v4.0.0 breaking change**: Task state representation was redesigned; older state files are incompatible
8. **Windows daemonization unreliable**: Before v4.0, `pueued --daemonize` on Windows could terminate if terminal closes

---

**Undocumented or vague**: Exact JSON schema for `pueue status --json` (whether it includes per-task `dependencies` array), stdout format of `pueue add --print-id`, explicit `--working-directory` flag (tasks run in "original working directories" but no CLI override found), stderr-only retrieval, and whether `pause_group_on_failure` config key name is exact.

Sources:
- [Get started · Nukesor/pueue Wiki](https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/wiki/Get-started)
- [Groups · Nukesor/pueue Wiki](https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/wiki/Groups)
- [Configuration · Nukesor/pueue Wiki](https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/wiki/Configuration)
- [pueue-add man page](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/pueue-add)
- [pueue-restart man page](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/pueue-restart)
- [pueue CHANGELOG](https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)
- [Pueue GitHub Repository](https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue)

# Pueue agent skill — implementation plan

## 1. Skill name + frontmatter

**Name:** `pueue-job-queue` (skip "orchestrator" — it overpromises a DAG engine; this is a CLI bridge)

**`description:`** (single line, trigger-rich):

> Drive Nukesor/pueue (https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue) for queued, parallel, scheduled, and lightly-DAG'd shell jobs from the agent — wraps `pueue add --after`, `pueue status --json`, `pueue log --json`, group-level parallelism, and `pueued` daemon health. Use when the user wants to background long-running shell commands across reboots, queue dozens of jobs with capped parallelism, run a fan-out / fan-in pipeline of shell steps, says "pueue", "pueued", "pueue add", "pueue queue", "pueue group", "task queue for shell", or asks how to schedule/parallelize CLI work without a real orchestrator (Airflow/Prefect/Dagster).

Trigger phrases (3+ in description above): "pueue", "queue dozens of jobs", "fan-out / fan-in", "task queue for shell", "schedule/parallelize CLI work".

## 2. SKILL.md outline (target ~220 lines body)

1. **Title + 1-paragraph mental model** — pueue = persistent shell job queue, daemon-backed, group = parallelism unit, `--after` = success-only AND deps.
2. **When to use** — long shell jobs, capped parallelism, fan-out/fan-in shell pipelines, "wait then run" sequencing, scheduled (`--delay`) / stashed jobs.
3. **When NOT to use** — needs cross-host scheduling → real orchestrator; needs OR/conditional/retry-on-fail deps → not pueue (`--after` is AND, success-only); needs typed task IO / artifacts → DVC or Prefect.
4. **Authoritative sources** — `https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue`, `man pueue`, `pueue --help`.
5. **Setup quickstart** — run `scripts/check-daemon.sh`; one-liner `pueued -d`; macOS launchd hint.
6. **Core mental model table** — task / group / daemon / config.
7. **Workflow A: submit one** — `scripts/submit.sh -- echo hi`.
8. **Workflow B: batch with shared group + capped parallelism** — `pueue group add ml`, `pueue parallel 4 --group ml`, then loop `submit.sh --group ml`.
9. **Workflow C: linear DAG** — `scripts/submit-dag.py dag.yaml` returns name→id map.
10. **Workflow D: wait** — `scripts/wait.py --ids 1,2,3` or `--label-prefix train-`.
11. **Workflow E: logs / retry / kill** — points at `pueue log --json`, `pueue restart --in-place`, `pueue kill && pueue remove`.
12. **Available scripts** — bullet list (3-line summary each).
13. **Reference files** — bullet list with "read when ..." trigger.
14. **Bundled assets** — `dag.example.yaml`, `pueue.yml.example`.
15. **Gotchas** (8 minimum, see §6 below for the empirical ones; non-empirical ones already certain):
    - `--after` is AND-only and success-only — failed parent → `DependencyFailed`, never runs.
    - Daemon must be running; `pueued -d` is opaque-failure if already running.
    - Default group always exists; new groups need `pueue parallel N --group X` or workers stay at 1.
    - `pause_group_on_failure` is config-only — no CLI flag.
    - `pueue restart` (default) makes a NEW task id; use `--in-place` to keep the slot.
    - Logs live in platform dirs (Linux/macOS/Windows) — `tail -f` won't find them in CWD.
    - `pueue clean` removes done tasks permanently; `--successful-only` is a flag, not default.
    - macOS daemon: `pueued -d` actually daemonizes cleanly (verify) — but no plist ships; user manages lifecycle.
    - Stdout of `pueue add --print-id` shape unverified — `submit.sh` parses defensively (regex grep for digits).

## 3. Scripts to ship

All under `skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/`. All chmod 0755, `set -euo pipefail`, bash 3.2 compat where bash, `--help` everywhere.

### `check-daemon.sh` (bash)

**Purpose:** Single-shot daemon health check + actionable install hint.
**Flags:** `--start` (auto-launch `pueued -d` if missing), `--json` (default on), `--help`.
**Stdout:** `{"daemon_running": true|false, "pueue_version": "3.4.1", "client_version": "3.4.1", "default_group": {"parallel_tasks": 1, "status": "Running"}, "platform": "darwin", "log_dir": "/Users/.../Library/Application Support/pueue/logs"}`
**Stderr:** Prose hints (`pueued not running — try: pueued -d`; or `version mismatch: client 3.4.1 vs daemon 3.3.0 — restart daemon`).
**Exit codes:** `0` healthy, `2` `pueue` CLI not installed, `3` daemon unreachable, `4` version mismatch.

### `submit.sh` (bash)

**Purpose:** Submit ONE task, return clean JSON. Wraps `pueue add --print-id`.
**Flags:** `--label TXT`, `--group G`, `--after ID` (repeatable), `--immediate`, `--stashed`, `--delay STR` (e.g. `10min`), `--priority N`, `--working-dir PATH`, `--escape`, `--dry-run`, `--help`. After `--`, the command.
**Stdout:** `{"task_id": 17, "label": "train-1", "group": "ml", "after": [12, 14], "immediate": false, "stashed": false}`
**Stderr:** `submitted task 17 (group=ml, after=[12,14])`.
**Exit codes:** `0` ok, `1` bad args, `2` pueue not installed, `3` `pueue add` failed (parent died, etc.), `4` daemon unreachable.
**Empirical:** parses `--print-id` output by capturing trailing integer with `grep -oE '[0-9]+$'` — falls back to immediate `pueue status --json | jq` lookup of last task by label if parse fails.

### `wait.py` (PEP 723, `uv run --script`)

**Purpose:** Block until a set of tasks reaches terminal status. Polls `pueue status --json`.
**Selectors (one required):** `--ids 1,2,3`, `--label LABEL` (exact, repeatable), `--label-prefix train-`, `--group ml`.
**Flags:** `--poll-seconds 2.0`, `--timeout-seconds 0` (0 = no timeout), `--fail-fast` (return non-zero the moment any selected task fails), `--quiet` (suppress per-tick stderr), `--help`.
**Stdout (terminal):** JSON object:
```json
{"summary": {"total": 4, "success": 3, "failed": 1, "killed": 0, "dependency_failed": 0},
 "tasks": [{"id": 17, "label": "train-1", "status": "Done", "exit_code": 0, "start": "...", "end": "...", "group": "ml"}],
 "elapsed_seconds": 42.3}
```
**Stderr:** One line per poll tick (`tick 12: 2 running, 1 queued, 1 done`); suppressed under `--quiet`.
**Exit codes:** `0` all selected tasks `Done` with exit 0; `1` arg error; `5` ≥1 task failed/killed/dependency_failed; `6` timeout; `4` daemon unreachable.
**Deps:** `pyyaml` (only if loading group filter from yaml — drop if unused). Realistically zero deps; uses `subprocess` + stdlib `json`.

### `submit-dag.py` (PEP 723, `uv run --script`)

**Purpose:** Submit a linear DAG (success-only deps). Topo-sorts, submits in order, wires `--after` from name→id map.
**Spec source:** Positional arg = path to YAML/JSON file, OR `-` for stdin (heredoc-friendly). **Decision: support both. Default = file, `-` = stdin.** Format detected by extension OR magic-sniff (`{` / `[` → JSON; else YAML). Stdin assumed YAML unless `--format json`.
**Flags:** `--format yaml|json|auto` (default `auto`), `--default-group GROUP`, `--label-prefix STR` (prepended to each task's `name` to form pueue label), `--dry-run` (print plan, submit nothing), `--print-graph` (also dump topo order to stderr), `--help`.
**Spec schema (YAML):**
```yaml
version: 1
default_group: ml
tasks:
  fetch:
    cmd: ./fetch.sh
    group: io          # optional; falls back to default_group
  featurize:
    cmd: python feat.py
    after: [fetch]
  train_a:
    cmd: python train.py --seed 1
    after: [featurize]
  train_b:
    cmd: python train.py --seed 2
    after: [featurize]
  evaluate:
    cmd: python eval.py
    after: [train_a, train_b]
```
**Stdout:** `{"tasks": {"fetch": 17, "featurize": 18, "train_a": 19, "train_b": 20, "evaluate": 21}, "topo_order": ["fetch", "featurize", "train_a", "train_b", "evaluate"], "default_group": "ml"}`
**Stderr:** Per-task submit prose (`fetch -> 17`, `featurize -> 18 (after=[17])`).
**Validation (before any submit):** unknown `after:` name, cycle, empty `tasks:`, missing `cmd:` → fail with `1` and a pointer to the offending key. **No partial submits** — pre-validate fully.
**Exit codes:** `0` all submitted; `1` schema error / cycle / unknown ref; `2` pueue not installed; `3` mid-run pueue failure (in which case stderr names the task that broke and stdout still emits whatever IDs DID get submitted, so the agent can clean up).
**Deps (PEP 723):** `pyyaml>=6`.

**Why 4 scripts and not more:** retry / kill / log-tail are one-line `pueue` calls — documenting them in `references/cli-cheatsheet.md` beats wrapping. A wrapper adds value only when it (a) reshapes output to JSON, (b) hides multi-step orchestration (DAG submit), or (c) blocks (wait). Single `pueue restart --in-place` and `pueue log --json` don't qualify.

Under `skills/local/pueue-job-queue/references/`. Each linked from SKILL.md with "read when ..." trigger.

One-line description + when to use.

Begins with: *"Run this once on your version (`pueue --version`) and diff:"*  followed by `pueue status --json | jq 'keys, .tasks | (keys | first as $k | .[$k])'`. Ships useful jq one-liners: get all running ids, get failed tasks with stderr path, group→pending count, dependents of task X.
- **`dag-patterns.md`** — fan-out / fan-in / mixed examples (matching `dag.example.yaml`); explicit limitations: AND-only, success-only, no OR, no conditional, no retry-on-fail; "when to fall back": >1 host, OR/conditional deps, typed artifacts, retries with backoff → use Prefect/Dagster/Airflow; mention DVC's `dvc exp run --queue` for ML-sweep workloads.

## 6. Known unknowns — verification checklist (run BEFORE finalizing scripts)

Run all of these on the implementer's machine, paste real output into a scratchpad, then code against what you actually see:

1. **`--print-id` format** — `pueue add --print-id -- echo hi` → is stdout a bare integer, JSON `{"task_id": N}`, or prose like `New task added (id 7)`? Decides `submit.sh`'s parse strategy.
2. **`status --json` key for deps** — `pueue add -- sleep 5 && pueue add --after 1 -- echo hi && pueue status --json | jq '.tasks["2"] | keys'` → confirm whether the field is `dependencies`, `dependency_ids`, or under `original_command` metadata. Hard-code in `wait.py` and `json-schema.md` examples.
3. **Failed-dep status string** — kill task 1 then check task 2's `.status`. Is it `DependencyFailed`, `Dependency_failed`, an object `{"DependencyFailed": ...}`, or nested under `Failed`? `wait.py`'s exit-code logic depends on this.
4. **`exit_code` location** — top-level on the task, or nested under a `result` / `status` object? Pueue serializes tagged enums via serde — likely `{"status": {"Done": {"exit_code": 0, "result": "Success"}}}` rather than flat. Confirm.
5. **macOS `pueued -d` daemonization** — does it fork cleanly and detach from terminal? If it stays foreground, `--start` flag in `check-daemon.sh` needs `nohup pueued -d </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &`.
6. **Default-group autocreate** — does referencing `--group new_name` on `pueue add` auto-create it, or fail? If fail, `submit.sh --group X` must check + `pueue group add X` first.
7. **Pre-existing task with same label** — does pueue dedupe by label, or allow duplicates? Affects whether `wait.py --label X` can match >1.
8. **Version compatibility** — `pueue --version` on the dev box. Note in `json-schema.md`. Re-verify schema if user is on a different major.

## Background from prior exploration (treat as ground truth)

### Pueue facts
- Daemon `pueued -d` must be running for any client command. No daemon → opaque error.
- `pueue add [--label TXT] [--group G] [--after ID]... [--immediate] [--stashed] [--delay 10min] [--priority N] [--print-id] [--escape] -- <cmd>` enqueues. `--after` is AND-only and **success-only**: failed parent → dependents marked `DependencyFailed` (do not run).
- Default group is `default` and always exists. Custom groups: `pueue group add <name>` then `pueue parallel <n> --group <name>`.
- `pueue status --json` and `pueue log --json` are the agent-friendly surfaces. Exact JSON schema for `dependencies`/`exit_code` keys is **not authoritatively documented** — the skill's helper scripts must `verify with --json | jq once and trust observed shape`, not paper-document it.
- `pueue restart [--in-place] [--start-immediately] <ids...>` — default creates a new task id; `--in-place` reuses the original id slot.
- Logs live in platform-specific dirs: Linux `~/.local/share/pueue/logs/`, macOS `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs/`, Windows `%APPDATA%\pueue\logs\`.
- Config file: `~/.config/pueue/pueue.yml` (Linux), `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/pueue.yml` (macOS). `pause_group_on_failure: true` is config-only (no CLI flag).
- `pueue add --print-id` outputs the new task id to stdout — format **not authoritatively documented** (probably plain int, must verify).

### User's prior art (PueueWrapper)
- The user's Python wrapper is **a thin CLI bridge**, not a custom scheduler. It wraps `--after` directly rather than building a custom DAG engine. Pydantic models parse `pueue status --json` into `Task`, `Group`, `PueueStatus` with helpers like `.get_running_tasks()`, `.get_done_tasks()`. Polling-based waits, no internal timeout in the public API. Group-level parallelism is the parallelism primitive — there is no per-task pool.

### Repo conventions (already verified)
- Local skills live at `skills/local/<name>/` with `SKILL.md`, `references/`, `scripts/`, `assets/`.
- Scripts must be executable (0755), bash 3.2 compatible, `set -euo pipefail`, support `--help` and (where applicable) `--dry-run`. **Stdout = structured data (JSON), stderr = prose diagnostics.**
- Python helpers use **PEP 723 inline-deps** + `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script`. Examples already in repo: `skills/local/mlflow-tracking/scripts/tail-runs.sh` (inspect for style).
- SKILL.md must have `name`, `description` frontmatter, "Use when ..." trigger phrases (3+), under 500 lines. `references/X.md` must each be linked from SKILL.md.
- Existing CLI-wrapper skills to mirror in shape: `skills/local/dvc-ml-workflow/` (subcommand-style queue helper) and `skills/local/mlflow-tracking/` (mix of bash + PEP 723 Python).
- Lint: `bash skills/local/skill-author/scripts/lint-skill.sh skills/local/<name>`.

```text
1	---
2	name: dvc-ml-workflow
3	description: Set up and operate a DVC (Data Version Control) workflow for ML projects — `dvc init`, `dvc.yaml` pipelines, `params.yaml`, `dvc exp run --queue` for parallel sweeps with metrics auto-bound to ephemeral git commits, and remote storage (S3/SSH/GDrive). Use whenever the user wants reproducible ML pipelines, data/model versioning that lives alongside git, parameter sweeps without standing up a tracking server, queued/parallel experiment execution, or asks about `dvc.yaml` / `dvc exp run` / `dvc queue` / `params.yaml` / `dvc add` / `dvc push` / `.dvc/cache`. Always references the official docs at https://dvc.org/doc and the upstream repo https://github.com/treeverse/dvc (Iterative was acquired by Treeverse in 2024 — `pip install dvc` resolves to this repo).
4	---
5	
6	# DVC ML Workflow
7	
8	DVC turns a git repo into a full ML lab: data and model files are versioned out-of-band (in a cache + remote), pipelines are declared in `dvc.yaml`, and experiments are run as ephemeral git commits with metrics and plots attached. No tracking server, no separate database — everything lives in your existing git history.
9	
10	This skill is opinionated about **the parts of DVC that matter for production ML work**: pipelines, queued experiments, metrics/commit binding, and remotes. It defers to the official docs at https://dvc.org/doc for everything else and links them inline so the agent always pulls the latest guidance.
11	
12	## When to use
13	
14	- User wants reproducible ML pipelines without a tracking server (`mlflow`, `wandb`, etc.)
15	- User mentions `dvc.yaml`, `params.yaml`, `dvc exp run`, `dvc queue`, `dvc push`, `.dvc/cache`
16	- User wants to do a hyperparameter sweep / grid search and have each run land as a separate commit with metrics
17	- User wants to version a dataset or model file too large for git
18	- User asks "how do I make my training reproducible" and is already on git
19	- User wants `mlflow ui`-style experiment comparison but **doesn't want to run a server** (DVC's `dvc exp show` + VS Code extension fills that role)
20	
21	## When NOT to use
22	
23	- User wants a hosted experiment dashboard with multi-user collaboration → use `mlflow-tracking` skill
24	- User wants LLM trace observability (spans, prompts, token costs) → DVC has no story here; use `mlflow-tracking`
25	- User just needs `git lfs` for a few large files → DVC is overkill; recommend `git lfs`
26	- User has an existing `mlflow` workflow and is happy with it → don't push DVC unless they ask
27	
28	## Authoritative sources (always link these, don't paraphrase from memory)
29	
30	- Docs root: https://dvc.org/doc
31	- Command reference: https://dvc.org/doc/command-reference
32	- User guide: https://dvc.org/doc/user-guide
33	- Upstream repo: https://github.com/treeverse/dvc (formerly `iterative/dvc`; redirects)
34	- PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/dvc/
35	
36	When you're unsure of a flag, syntax, or behavior, **fetch the relevant doc page** rather than guessing — DVC's CLI surface changes between minor versions.
37	
38	## Core mental model
39	
40	Three orthogonal things, often confused:
41	
42	| DVC concept | Analogy | What it does |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| `dvc add <file>` | `git lfs track` | Snapshots a single file/dir into the cache, writes a `.dvc` pointer file (which **is** committed to git) |
45	| `dvc.yaml` (stages) | `Makefile` | Declares pipeline stages with dependencies and outputs; `dvc repro` re-runs only stages whose inputs changed |
46	| `dvc exp run` | `git commit` for experiments | Runs the pipeline once with optional param overrides, captures metrics + outputs as an **ephemeral commit** |
47	
48	The non-obvious bit: `dvc exp run` builds on top of `dvc.yaml`. You don't choose between "use pipelines" and "run experiments" — you write the pipeline once, then launch many experiments against it.
49	
50	## Workflow
51	
52	### 1. Initialize the project
53	
54	Use the bundled helper (handles `.gitignore`, sample files, optional remote):
55	
56	```bash
57	bash skills/local/dvc-ml-workflow/scripts/init-dvc-project.sh
58	# or with a remote:
59	bash skills/local/dvc-ml-workflow/scripts/init-dvc-project.sh --remote s3://my-bucket/dvc-store
60	```
61	
62	Manual equivalent (only do this if the helper doesn't fit):
63	
64	```bash
65	dvc init                              # creates .dvc/, .dvcignore
66	git add .dvc .dvcignore
67	git commit -m "Initialize DVC"
68	```
69	
70	For a sub-project inside a monorepo that already has its own `.git`, use `dvc init --subdir`. See [Gotchas](#gotchas).
71	
72	### 2. Track data and models
73	
74	```bash
75	dvc add data/raw/             # snapshot a directory
76	dvc add models/best.pt        # snapshot a single model file
77	git add data/raw.dvc models/best.pt.dvc .gitignore
78	git commit -m "Track raw data and best model"
79	```
80	
81	The `.dvc` files are tiny pointers (md5 + path). The actual bytes go to `.dvc/cache/`. **Never** `git add` anything inside `.dvc/cache/` — it's gitignored automatically and would defeat the purpose.
82	
83	### 3. Define a pipeline (`dvc.yaml`)
84	
85	Use `params.yaml` for hyperparameters. Use `dvc stage add` to declare stages — never hand-edit `dvc.yaml` from scratch unless you've already used `dvc stage add` enough times to know the schema.
86	
87	```bash
88	dvc stage add -n featurize \
89	  -d src/featurize.py -d data/raw \
90	  -o data/features \
91	  python src/featurize.py
92	
93	dvc stage add -n train \
94	  -d src/train.py -d data/features -p model.lr,model.epochs \
95	  -o models/best.pt \
96	  -M metrics.json --plots-no-cache plots.csv \
97	  python src/train.py
98	```
99	
100	The `-M` flag marks a file as a **metrics file** (auto-bound to the experiment commit). `--plots-no-cache` marks a file as a plot source (rendered by `dvc plots show`).
101	
102	For schema details and `foreach` matrix stages, **read** `references/pipelines-and-stages.md`.
103	
104	### 4. Run experiments (the queue is the killer feature)
105	
106	For a single run:
107	
108	```bash
109	dvc exp run                           # uses current params.yaml
110	dvc exp run -S model.lr=1e-3          # override one param
111	dvc exp run -S 'model.lr=range(1e-4,1e-2,3)'  # NOT valid — see queue below
112	```
113	
114	For a **sweep**, queue + start workers:
115	
116	```bash
117	# Enqueue a grid (each -S adds one experiment to the queue):
118	dvc exp run --queue -S model.lr=1e-4
119	dvc exp run --queue -S model.lr=5e-4
120	dvc exp run --queue -S model.lr=1e-3
121	
122	# Start 3 parallel workers — they each pick one queued experiment:
123	dvc queue start --jobs 3
124	
125	# Watch progress:
126	dvc queue status
127	dvc queue logs <task-id>             # if one fails
128	
129	# When done:
130	dvc exp show                          # tabular view of all experiments
131	```
132	
133	Each completed experiment is an **ephemeral commit** in `refs/exps/...`. Metrics, params, and outputs are bundled with it. Promote one to a real commit with `dvc exp apply <exp-name>` then `git commit`.
134	
135	For grids, queue helpers, and ephemeral-vs-real commit semantics, **read** `references/experiments-and-queue.md`.
136	
137	### 5. Push artifacts to a remote
138	
139	```bash
140	dvc remote add -d origin s3://my-bucket/dvc-store    # -d = default
141	dvc push                                             # upload cache to remote
142	git push                                             # share the .dvc pointers
143	```
144	
145	Anyone who clones can `dvc pull` to get the actual bytes. For S3 / GCS / Azure / SSH / GDrive specifics and credential handling, **read** `references/data-and-remotes.md`.
146	
147	### 6. Compare and visualize
148	
149	```bash
150	dvc exp show                          # table of all experiments
151	dvc exp show --csv | column -t -s,    # human-readable
152	dvc metrics show                      # current workspace metrics
153	dvc metrics diff HEAD~1               # compare against last commit
154	dvc plots show                        # render plots from --plots files
155	dvc plots diff HEAD~1                 # overlay current vs prior plots
156	```
157	
158	For plot templates (Vega-Lite), confusion matrices, and the VS Code extension, **read** `references/plots-and-metrics.md`.
159	
160	## Available scripts
161	
162	- **`scripts/init-dvc-project.sh`** — Idempotent project init. `dvc init` + `.gitignore` for `.dvc/cache/` + optional `dvc remote add` + drops the `dvc.yaml` / `params.yaml` / `.dvcignore` templates from `assets/` if missing.
163	  - Flags: `--remote URL`, `--subdir`, `--force`, `--dry-run`, `--help`
164	- **`scripts/queue-helper.sh`** — Wraps `dvc queue` subcommands with structured JSON stdout (one object per task) so an agent can grep/filter task status without parsing tabular output.
165	  - Subcommands: `enqueue PARAM=VAL,...`, `start --jobs N`, `status`, `logs TASK_ID`
166	  - Flags: `--help`, `--json` (default for `status`)
167	- **`scripts/lint-dvcyaml.sh`** — Validates `dvc.yaml` by running `dvc dag --dot` (parse-only, no execution). Exits non-zero with the parse error if the schema is broken.
168	  - Flags: `--help`
169	
170	## Bundled assets
171	
172	- `assets/dvc.yaml.template` — Minimal 2-stage pipeline (`featurize` → `train`) with metrics and plots wired up correctly.
173	- `assets/params.yaml.template` — Nested params for `data` / `model` / `train` sections (the `-S model.lr=...` override syntax keys off this nesting).
174	- `assets/.dvcignore.template` — Sensible defaults: ignore notebooks, scratch dirs, `__pycache__`, etc.
175	
176	## Reference files
177	
178	- `references/pipelines-and-stages.md` — Read **when** writing or debugging `dvc.yaml`: stage schema, `foreach`, `vars`, `wdir`, `frozen`, `always_changed`, and the difference between `-d` / `-o` / `-M` / `--plots`.
179	- `references/experiments-and-queue.md` — Read **when** the user wants sweeps, parallel runs, or asks how metrics get bound to commits. Covers `dvc exp run --queue`, `dvc queue start --jobs`, `dvc exp apply` / `branch` / `remove` / `gc`, and ephemeral-commit semantics.
180	- `references/data-and-remotes.md` — Read **when** setting up `dvc remote` or troubleshooting `dvc push` / `dvc pull`. Covers S3, SSH, GDrive, Azure, GCS, MinIO (S3-compatible), credentials via env / `dvc remote modify --local`.
181	- `references/plots-and-metrics.md` — Read **when** the user asks about visualization, dashboards, or VS Code integration. Covers `dvc plots show / diff`, custom Vega-Lite templates, confusion matrices, and `dvc.api.metrics_show()` for programmatic access.
182	
183	## Gotchas
184	
185	- **`dvc init` fails inside an existing repo's subdirectory** unless you pass `--subdir`. Symptom: `ERROR: '.git' or '.hg' directory not found`. The helper script handles this — manually, do `dvc init --subdir`.
186	- **`dvc exp run --queue` only enqueues; it does not run.** Until you call `dvc queue start`, queued experiments sit idle. The agent will sometimes report "experiment finished" because the enqueue succeeded — verify with `dvc queue status`.
187	- **`dvc.lock` MUST be committed.** It records the exact md5s of inputs/outputs for each stage. If you `.gitignore` it, `dvc repro` becomes non-deterministic between machines. Conversely, **`.dvc/cache/` MUST NOT be committed** (it's the actual data — that goes to the remote).
188	- **Metrics file format matters.** `-M metrics.json` expects a flat JSON object (`{"acc": 0.91, "loss": 0.3}`) or a one-level-nested one. YAML works too. Free-form text won't render in `dvc exp show`.
189	- **`dvc push` silently succeeds if the remote is misconfigured but credentials are missing** for some backends — it just reports "0 files pushed" without an error code in older versions. Always verify with `dvc status -c` (cloud status) after the first push from a new machine.
190	- **Param overrides use dot-notation against `params.yaml` keys.** `-S lr=1e-3` only works if `lr` is at the top level. If you nested it under `model:`, you must use `-S model.lr=1e-3`.
191	- **macOS port 8080 / Iterative Studio**: if the user mentions Iterative Studio, note that it's now a separate Treeverse-managed product, not bundled with `dvc` itself. Don't conflate the two.
192	- **`dvc queue start` runs jobs in the background.** Closing your terminal does NOT kill them (they're detached). Use `dvc queue kill <task-id>` to stop one.
193
```

```text
1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# queue-helper.sh — Agent-friendly wrapper around `dvc queue` and `dvc exp run --queue`.
3	#
4	# Stdout is structured (JSON), stderr is prose. Designed for an LLM caller.
5	#
6	# Bash 3.2 compatible (works on stock macOS).
7	
8	set -euo pipefail
9	
10	usage() {
11	  cat <<'EOF'
12	Usage: queue-helper.sh [GLOBAL OPTIONS] <subcommand> [ARGS]
13	
14	Wraps `dvc queue` / `dvc exp run --queue` with structured JSON stdout.
15	
16	Subcommands:
17	  enqueue PARAM=VAL[,PARAM=VAL...] [...]   Enqueue one experiment per arg group.
18	                                           Each ARG is comma-joined param overrides.
19	  grid PARAM=VAL1,VAL2 [PARAM=VAL1,VAL2]   Cartesian-product grid sweep.
20	  start [--jobs N]                         Start the worker pool (default: 1).
21	  status                                   Print queue status as JSON array.
22	  logs TASK_ID                             Stream logs of one queued/running task.
23	  stop                                     Stop worker pool (queued tasks survive).
24	  clear                                    Remove all queued (not-yet-started) tasks.
25	
26	Global options:
27	  --dry-run          Show what would be enqueued/started; don't run.
28	  --help, -h         Show this help and exit.
29	
30	Examples:
31	  # Enqueue 3 explicit experiments:
32	  queue-helper.sh enqueue model.lr=1e-4 model.lr=5e-4 model.lr=1e-3
33	
34	  # 2x3 grid (6 experiments enqueued):
35	  queue-helper.sh grid model.lr=1e-4,5e-4,1e-3 train.batch_size=32,64
36	
37	  # Start 4 workers and wait:
38	  queue-helper.sh start --jobs 4
39	
40	  # Check what's queued:
41	  queue-helper.sh status
42	
43	Exit codes:
44	  0  success
45	  1  invalid arguments
46	  2  dvc CLI not installed
47	  3  dvc command failed
48	EOF
49	}
50	
51	log()  { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; }
52	die()  { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit "${2:-1}"; }
53	
54	DRY_RUN=0
55	
56	# Pre-parse global flags before subcommand.
57	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
58	  case "$1" in
59	    --dry-run) DRY_RUN=1; shift ;;
60	    --help|-h) usage; exit 0 ;;
61	    --) shift; break ;;
62	    -*) die "unknown global flag: $1 (try --help)" 1 ;;
63	    *)  break ;;
64	  esac
65	done
66	
67	[ $# -gt 0 ] || die "missing subcommand (try --help)" 1
68	command -v dvc >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "dvc not found in PATH" 2
69	
70	SUB="$1"; shift
71	
72	run_dvc() {
73	  if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
74	    log "[dry-run] dvc $*"
75	    return 0
76	  fi
77	  dvc "$@" || die "dvc $* failed" 3
78	}
79	
80	# Build -S flags from a comma-separated list like "model.lr=1e-4,train.bs=32".
81	build_s_flags() {
82	  local spec="$1" out=""
83	  local IFS=','
84	  for kv in $spec; do
85	    [ -n "$kv" ] || continue
86	    out="$out -S $kv"
87	  done
88	  printf '%s' "$out"
89	}
90	
91	case "$SUB" in
92	  enqueue)
93	    [ $# -gt 0 ] || die "enqueue: provide at least one PARAM=VAL spec" 1
94	    count=0
95	    for spec in "$@"; do
96	      flags=$(build_s_flags "$spec")
97	      if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
98	        log "[dry-run] dvc exp run --queue$flags"
99	      else
100	        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
101	        dvc exp run --queue $flags || die "enqueue failed for: $spec" 3
102	      fi
103	      count=$((count + 1))
104	    done
105	    printf '{"action":"enqueue","enqueued":%d}\n' "$count"
106	    ;;
107	
108	  grid)
109	    [ $# -gt 0 ] || die "grid: provide at least one PARAM=V1,V2,... axis" 1
110	
111	    # Cartesian product. Bash 3.2 has no associative arrays; build incrementally.
112	    # Combos starts as one empty combo "".
113	    combos=""
114	    first=1
115	    for axis in "$@"; do
116	      key="${axis%%=*}"
117	      vals="${axis#*=}"
118	      [ "$key" = "$axis" ] && die "grid axis missing '=': $axis" 1
119	
120	      new_combos=""
121	      IFS=','
122	      for v in $vals; do
123	        [ -n "$v" ] || continue
124	        if [ "$first" = "1" ]; then
125	          item="${key}=${v}"
126	          new_combos="${new_combos}|${item}"
127	        else
128	          # Append "${key}=${v}" to every existing combo.
129	          IFS='|'
130	          for existing in $combos; do
131	            [ -n "$existing" ] || continue
132	            new_combos="${new_combos}|${existing},${key}=${v}"
133	          done
134	          IFS=','
135	        fi
136	      done
137	      unset IFS
138	      combos="$new_combos"
139	      first=0
140	    done
141	
142	    count=0
143	    IFS='|'
144	    for combo in $combos; do
145	      [ -n "$combo" ] || continue
146	      flags=$(build_s_flags "$combo")
147	      if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
148	        log "[dry-run] dvc exp run --queue$flags"
149	      else
150	        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
151	        dvc exp run --queue $flags || die "enqueue failed for combo: $combo" 3
152	      fi
153	      count=$((count + 1))
154	    done
155	    unset IFS
156	    printf '{"action":"grid","enqueued":%d}\n' "$count"
157	    ;;
158	
159	  start)
160	    JOBS=1
161	    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
162	      case "$1" in
163	        --jobs) JOBS="${2:-1}"; shift 2 ;;
164	        *) die "start: unexpected arg $1" 1 ;;
165	      esac
166	    done
167	    run_dvc queue start --jobs "$JOBS"
168	    printf '{"action":"start","jobs":%d}\n' "$JOBS"
169	    ;;
170	
171	  status)
172	    if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
173	      log "[dry-run] dvc queue status"
174	      printf '{"action":"status","tasks":[]}\n'
175	      exit 0
176	    fi
177	    # `dvc queue status` outputs human-readable text; capture and re-emit raw under "raw"
178	    # plus structured stub. Future: parse properly when dvc gains --json.
179	    raw=$(dvc queue status 2>&1 || true)
180	    # Escape for JSON.
181	    raw_esc=$(printf '%s' "$raw" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g' -e ':a;N;$!ba;s/\n/\\n/g')
182	    printf '{"action":"status","raw":"%s"}\n' "$raw_esc"
183	    ;;
184	
185	  logs)
186	    [ $# -gt 0 ] || die "logs: TASK_ID required" 1
187	    TASK_ID="$1"
188	    if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
189	      log "[dry-run] dvc queue logs $TASK_ID"
190	      exit 0
191	    fi
192	    dvc queue logs "$TASK_ID"
193	    ;;
194	
195	  stop)
196	    run_dvc queue stop
197	    printf '{"action":"stop"}\n'
198	    ;;
199	
200	  clear)
201	    if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
202	      log "[dry-run] dvc queue remove --all --queued"
203	    else
204	      dvc queue remove --queued || true
205	    fi
206	    printf '{"action":"clear"}\n'
207	    ;;
208	
209	  *)
210	    die "unknown subcommand: $SUB (try --help)" 1
211	    ;;
212	esac
213
```
</details></tool-use>

33

40	        "--experiment",

47	        help="MLflow tracking URI (default: $MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI).",

79	def main() -> int:
80	    args = parse_args()
81	
82	    if args.tracking_uri:

87	              file=sys.stderr)

93	            max_results=args.top_n,

98	        return 3
99

101	        print(f"warn: no runs found for experiment '{args.experiment}'", file=sys.stderr)
102	        df = pd.DataFrame()
103	
104	    if args.columns:
105	        cols = [c.strip() for c in args.columns.split(",") if c.strip()]
106	        missing = [c for c in cols if c not in df.columns]
107	        if missing:
108	            print(f"warn: missing columns ignored: {missing}", file=sys.stderr)
109	        cols = [c for c in cols if c in df.columns]
110	        df = df[cols] if cols else df
111

114	    else:
115	        # JSON: emit a list of objects (more agent-friendly than DataFrame.to_json).
116	        records = json.loads(df.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso"))
117	        print(json.dumps(records, indent=2, default=str))
118	
119	    print(f"returned {len(df)} run(s)", file=sys.stderr)
